summary: Defines a new attribute for the Telephony Routing over IP protocol to indicate telephone network services offering prioritized call setup, such as government emergency calling schemes. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: In an emergency, some calls get to go first. This lets phone-routing gateways advertise that they can handle those priority calls.

questions: what is the trip resource priority attribute
how do gateways advertise priority call support
what is telephony routing over ip
subtitle: A TRIP attribute that lets telephony gateways advertise which Resource-Priority namespaces they support.

tldr.problem: SIP can signal call priority with the Resource-Priority header, but TRIP had no way to advertise which gateways support a given priority namespace.
tldr.mechanism: A new optional TRIP attribute, ResourcePriority (type code 12), carries one or more NameSpace tokens, each as a length plus the namespace value.
tldr.outcome: Location Servers can now learn and spread which gateways reach PSTN services with prioritized call setup, such as GETS in the U.S. and GTPS in the U.K.

today: RFC 5115 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction to TRIP
sections.content:
An IP telephony gateway lets nodes on an IP network talk to the circuit-switched telephone network. The Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP) protocol, defined in RFC 3219, helps nodes find a suitable gateway through Location Servers. TRIP is a policy-driven, inter-administrative domain protocol for advertising the reachability of gateways, negotiating capabilities and specifying attributes.

TRIP is modeled after BGP-4 (RFC 4271) and uses path-vector advertisements passed hop by hop. Location Servers are grouped into administrative clusters called Internet Telephony Administrative Domains (ITADs). This RFC defines one new attribute, registered with IANA.
sections.eli5: TRIP is like a directory that tells phone systems which doors lead out to the regular phone network. This RFC adds one more thing the directory can say.

sections.title: Priority Calls and the SIP Resource-Priority Header
sections.content:
Emergency Telecommunications Service covers systems that support emergency communications. In the U.S., the Government Emergency Telecommunications Service (GETS) operates over the PSTN as a pay-per-use system for authorized personnel. It signals the National Security / Emergency Preparedness codepoint in an ISUP Initial Address Message, using the ANSI T1.631-1993 standard. Other priority standards named include ITU H.460.4 for H.323 calls and I.255.3 for multi-level precedence and preemption.

For SIP, the requirements in RFC 3487 led to the optional Resource-Priority header in RFC 4412. It has two parts: a NameSpace that identifies a group of priorities, and a Value that picks one priority in that set. The text lists three benefits: priority can be signaled to other entities, codepoints from other standards can map to NameSpace.Value tokens, and new namespaces can be defined without relying on a single set of priorities.
sections.eli5: Some callers, like emergency workers, have a special pass. SIP can carry a note saying which kind of pass a call has, and the note names a group of passes and one level inside it.

sections.title: The Gap in TRIP
sections.content: Once priority can be signaled through gateways, the next question is how to find which gateways support a given NameSpace. Spreading that kind of information is within the scope of TRIP. However, the TRIP specification at the time had no component that advertises associations of gateways with specific NameSpaces. The new attribute closes that omission by associating one or more NameSpaces with a gateway.
sections.eli5: Knowing how to ask for a priority call is not enough. You also need to know which gateway will honor it, and the directory had no place to say so.

sections.title: The ResourcePriority Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute follows the form of existing attributes in Section 5 of RFC 3219. Its flags are: Conditional Mandatory false, Required Flags Not Well-Known and Independent Transitive, Potential Flags none, and TRIP Type Code 12. It is optional, like the SIP header it mirrors, so it is Not Well-Known. Independent Transitive means it is forwarded among all ITADs, and a Location Server that does not recognize it sets the Partial flag.

The attribute carries one or more NameSpace token identifiers. Its syntax is copied from the namespace token of RFC 4412: one or more characters, each alphanumeric or one of a small set of punctuation marks listed in that RFC. Because namespaces vary in length, each tuple is a NameSpace Length followed by the NameSpace Value, with no padding between tuples.

The r-priority token of RFC 4412 is NOT used. The attribute advertises the namespace associated with a gateway, not the individual priorities inside it.
sections.eli5: Each entry is a name tag: first how long the name is, then the name itself. The sign lists which groups of priorities a gateway handles, not each single level.

sections.title: Origination, Aggregation and Dissemination
sections.content:
Three further TRIP considerations are covered. For route origination, if a route has a ResourcePriority attribute, the Location Server MUST include it in the advertisement it originates.

For route aggregation, routes with differing ResourcePriority token values MUST NOT be aggregated. Routes with the same token values MAY be aggregated, and the same attribute is attached to the result.

For dissemination and scope, a Location Server MUST include the attribute when talking to peers in its own domain. If it receives the attribute from a peer in another domain, it MUST propagate it to other servers in its domain. It MAY add the attribute when sending routing objects to another domain, which is a matter of local administrative policy.
sections.eli5: Gateways with different priority signs must not be lumped together, since a caller would not know which one to trust. Inside your own organization the sign is always shared, but sharing it outside is your choice.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document says the new attribute has no direct security considerations. The security considerations for TRIP and its messages remain as in Section 14 of RFC 3219.

For IANA, one new TRIP attribute is defined: code 12, named ResourcePriority. It is recorded in the IANA trip-parameters registry.
sections.eli5: The new sign adds no new dangers, so the old TRIP safety rules still cover it. It also got its official number, 12, in the public list.
